summary: PerfAgent wraps Mini-SWE-Agent in a controller that feeds a curated py-spy profiler summary (including native-extension frames), re-profiles after each passing patch for up to 5 iterations, runs affected tests via pytest-testmon, and keeps the fastest correct patch. On GSO (102 tasks) and SWE-fficiency-Lite (100 tasks) with GPT-5.1 it roughly doubles expert-matching (hack-adjusted) patches over the benchmark-provided OpenHands patches and beats an oracle best-of-5 OpenHands at lower cost.

claims.claim: PerfAgent raises hack-adjusted expert-matching rate from 19.6% to 39.2% on GSO and 26% to 74% on SWE-fficiency-Lite with GPT-5.1
claims.evidence: Table II: OpenHands Hack-Adj 19.6 / 26 vs PerfAgent 39.2 / 74; Codex 17.7 / 39. Single run; OpenHands numbers come from patches shipped with each benchmark rather than re-runs under the same $5/200-step budget, so budget parity with the 5-iteration PerfAgent is not controlled in this table.

claims.claim: Gains come from better feedback, not more test-time compute (beats oracle best@5 at lower cost)
claims.evidence: Table VI: GSO Hack-adj 39.2 vs OpenHands best@5 26.5 at $2.88 vs $11.01; SWE-fficiency-Lite 74 vs 68 at $4.25 vs $9.91. Oracle uses hidden tests, which favors the baseline. But the best@5 baseline is a different harness (OpenHands) from PerfAgent's base (Mini-SWE-Agent), and the A_L loop-only ablation on SWE-fficiency-Lite already reaches 46, so the compute-vs-feedback split is only partly isolated.

claims.claim: Profiler + test feedback together drive the improvement; tests alone do not help
claims.evidence: Table II ablation: GSO A_L 29.4, +Tests 20.6, +Profiler 34.4, PerfAgent 39.2; SWE-fficiency-Lite 46/46/57/74. Single run; GSO differences of a few points are a handful of tasks.

Table III: 27 vs 7 decisive tasks on GSO, 52 vs 4 on SWE-fficiency-Lite. §VI asserts significance, but no test statistic or p-value is reported (the counts would plausibly pass a sign test, but the paper does not show it).

claims.claim: Prompting the agent with profiler instructions is not a substitute for a harness-run curated profiler
claims.evidence: Table VII: A_P GSO Hack-Adj 16.7 vs PerfAgent 39.2; SWE-fficiency-Lite 44 vs 74.

patterns.note: Execution/timing/test verifier loop with best-patch retention beats one-shot agents and oracle best@5 (Tables II, VI).
Built on a single-agent Mini-SWE-Agent loop; gains come from harness-injected feedback, not multi-agent structure.
Deterministic tool output (profiler hotspots) summarized and injected beats prompting the agent to use the tool itself (Table VII).
$5/task cap truncates iterations on SWE-fficiency-Lite; $10 raises Hack-Adj 74→77 (Table IX). Cost reported per task in Table VI.
Evaluated on GSO and SWE-fficiency-Lite; documents reward hacking (18 of A_L's high-scoring patches flagged as hacks) when timing harness is naive (§IV-E4).
Uses GSO's LLM-as-judge hack detector combined with SWE-fficiency's detector, with manual review of flagged instances (§IV-A2, §VI).

methodology.sample: GSO 102 tasks / 10 repos; SWE-fficiency-Lite 100 tasks / 9 repos (random subset used by benchmark authors)
methodology.baselines: OpenHands patches distributed with each benchmark (not re-run), Codex run by authors, oracle OpenHands best@5, prompt-only profiler agent A_P, and component ablations
methodology.variance: Single run per configuration (§VI acknowledges); no CIs; significance asserted for Table III without a reported test
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; GSO hidden perf tests reduce workload overfitting; hack detection for reward hacking
methodology.languages: Python repositories with C/C++/Cython/Rust native extensions

standards.artifacts: Prompt given in Appendix A; no code repository for PerfAgent found in the text

biases.detail: All results single-run (§VI); Kimi-K2 GSO gap is ~2 tasks.
OpenHands baseline is the benchmark-supplied patch set, likely one-shot and not budget-matched to PerfAgent's 5 iterations; mitigated partly by oracle best@5 and A_L ablation.
Python-centric repos only; selective testing via pytest-testmon is Python-specific.
No PerfAgent code link; only the prompt is published.
SWE-fficiency-Lite times only the provided script, which authors show is gameable; headline 74% is on the weaker-validated benchmark.

verdict_reason: Ablations and a budget-aware oracle best@5 comparison make the 'feedback beats sampling' claim credible, but results are single-run, Python-only, the main baseline is not budget-matched, and code is not released.
applicability: Transferable as a harness pattern rather than a tool: for a Java ingestion/delivery stack, the lesson is that the harness (not the prompt) should run deterministic tools (a JFR/async-profiler summary, affected-test selection via something like Gradle test impact or Maven incremental tests) and feed curated results back, with a controller that retains the best verified patch. Nothing here is validated on Java, multi-repo changes, or spec-driven workflows; the reward-hacking finding (caching inside timing loops) is a concrete warning for any performance gate the team adds to its harness.
